title: Kernel-choice seqlen-mix correlation notes
content:
High-level goal:
This doc captures an ad-hoc experiment series investigating how sequence-length distribution in mixed production-like traffic influences the serving runtime's kernel selection (FlashAttention vs paged attention vs fused-op paths) and the downstream tail latency behavior. Intuition: kernel-selection heuristics tuned on homogeneous benchmarks (fixed seqlen) may pick suboptimal kernels under mixed loads, causing p99 regressions even when p50 looks fine.

Context / why now:
- Multiple customers saw elevated p99 on chat workloads after enabling a new fusion pass (PR 4321).
- SRE trace samples show correlations between long sequences interleaved with short queries and attention kernel handoffs (kernel-swap events).
- We need a small, reproducible bench that mimics our traffic mix to validate heuristics.

What I did (summary):
- Built a microbench harness (tools/seqmix_bench.py) that can replay a Poisson mix of sequence lengths and measure kernel selection counts, p50/p95/p99 latency, and device utilization on A100/H100.
- Instrumented runtime to log: (1) chosen kernel id, (2) input seqlen, (3) kv-cache hit/priming, (4) time at kernel handoff. Logs written to /tmp/seqmix-trace-<run>.ndjson.
- Ran 3 baseline workload shapes: 
  * W1: short-heavy (80% <= 64 tokens, 20% 512 tokens)
  * W2: balanced (50% 64, 30% 256, 20% 1024)
  * W3: long-heavy bursty (30% 32, 40% 512, 30% 2048) with bursts (lambda spike).
- Tested kernels: FlashAttention2 (FA2), PagedAttentionV1 (PA), and our fused-attn fallback (FUSED-ATTN, older path).

Benchmark env:
- Image: inference-runtime:canary-2025-02
- GPUs: A100-40GB (node-a), H100-80GB (node-b) for cross-check
- Batch sizes: single-request (1) as well as small sync batches (4).
- Measurement: 10k requests per shape, warmup 2k requests. Collected nsys traces for representative windows.

Key results (p50/p95/p99 in ms, kernel selection percentages in parentheses):
- W1 (short-heavy) on A100:
  * p50: 8ms, p95: 18ms, p99: 42ms
  * Kernel pick: FA2 92%, PA 6%, FUSED 2%
- W2 (balanced) on A100:
  * p50: 11ms, p95: 34ms, p99: 110ms
  * Kernel pick: FA2 61%, PA 27%, FUSED 12%
- W3 (long-heavy bursty) on A100:
  * p50: 28ms, p95: 120ms, p99: 420ms (observed long-tail spikes correlated with kernel handoffs)
  * Kernel pick: PA 54%, FA2 21%, FUSED 25%
- H100 observations (W2): p99 improved ~15% overall for FA2-heavy segments but PA shows similar tail growth during bursts.

Notable qualitative observations:
- Kernel handoff penalty: When the scheduler switches from FA2 to PA within a request burst, we see a ~60-120ms additional latency for the first request that triggers the handoff on A100. The handoff includes prefetch priming + different kernel cold paths.
- KV-cache priming: Long sequences frequently miss initial kv-cache, causing larger memory traffic; PA's paged layout reduces peak memory footprint but introduces page management overhead that surfaces in tails when interleaved with short queries.
- Fusion instability: FUSED-ATTN had lower p50 on isolated long runs but showed scatter (higher variance p99) in mixed mixes — likely due to register-pressure-induced slowdowns on some attention shapes.
- Small-batch coalescing: With batch=4 coalescing enabled, tails reduced ~12% for W2 but coalescer sometimes groups incompatible seqlens leading to inefficient kernel choices (fallback to FUSED).

Trace evidence snapshot (paraphrased):
- nsys window around p99 spike: kernel-call timestamps show FA2 kernel executed for one request, then a PA kernel invocation 3ms later for another request; scheduler paused to reallocate scratch buffers, causing a 78ms stall on the queue.
- Logs: "kernel_handoff event: from=FA2 to=PA cause=seqlen_jump priming_pages=42" repeated preceding many p99 samples.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Kernel selection threshold tuned on median seqlen isn't robust to heavy seqlen variance; handoff cost causes tail spikes in mixed bursts.
2) PA's page-management has non-linear overhead when interleaved with FA2 due to scratchpad reinit; this is exacerbated on A100 vs H100.
3) Fused-op path has register pressure cases that blow up latency for specific head-count/hidden-dim shapes when mixed.

Quick checks (to validate hypotheses):
- Re-run W2 and W3 with kernel-affinity pinning flags (force_FA2, force_PA) to see if p99 goes down (if forcing a single kernel avoids handoff cost).
- Add per-kernel pre-allocation of scratch buffer pools to reduce handoff allocation latency.
- Tune coalescer to avoid grouping sequences with >4x length ratio.

Preliminary mitigation experiments (results):
- force_FA2 on W2: p99 reduced from 110ms -> 78ms, but some long requests increased p50 for >1024 sequences (FA2 memory blowout).
- preallocated scratch pool (prototype): reduced handoff penalty from ~78ms -> ~22ms in a micro-run (W3 burst window). This looks promising.
- coalescer-length-ratio cap (<=4x): reduced FUSED fallback rate by ~40% and improved W2 p99 by 9%.

Action items (short-term):
- [ ] Add kernel-affinity experiment to CI perf registry (INF-2187) to run nightly on mixed-seqlen traces.
- [ ] Implement and run preallocated scratchpool across kernels (PR-xxxx). Benchmark memory overhead vs latency savings.
- [ ] Adjust coalescer heuristic: add seqlen_ratio cap and an isolation hint for outlier long requests.
- [ ] Instrument runtime to emit combined metric: kernel_handoff_rate / 1k reqs and avg_handoff_cost_ms. Surface in Console dashboard per-model.
- [ ] Ship a canary with scratchpool enabled for a subset of Dedicated customers and monitor tail.

Open questions / risks:
- Memory overhead for preallocation on H100: will preallocating scratch for both FA2 and PA exceed device memory when customers use very large models? Need safety fallback.
- Is forcing a single kernel ever acceptable for multi-tenant Dedicated clusters? Could cause capacity regressions.
- Do we need a predictive scheduler (lookahead based on recent seqlen samples) instead of reactive handoffs? Complexity vs benefit tradeoff.

Notes to self / TODOs inside the doc (rough):
- capture full nsys traces and link: /artifacts/seqmix/nsys-w3-burst-2025-02-11.zip
- write up simple flame-chart snippet for kernel handoff path (ask Diego for help)
- validate with additional headcount dims (8-heads vs 16-heads) — some fused cases look headcount-sensitive

Appendix: quick commands used
- run bench: python tools/seqmix_bench.py --shape W2 --gpu a100 --parallelism 64 --warmup 2000 --samples 10000 --out /tmp/w2-a100.log
- collect nsys: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output /tmp/nsys-w2 
  python tools/seqmix_bench.py --shape W2 --nsys-window 120 --samples 2000

Relevant tickets / PRs to reference:
- INF-2187: seq-mix nightly perf registry (tracking)
- PR 4321: experimental fusion pass (recent rollback flagged by CS)
- GH-#4279: initial paged-attn impl (Luca)

Bottom line (working conclusion):
Mixed sequence-length traffic exposes kernel handoff and page-management interactions that inflate p99. Short-term wins: preallocated scratch pools + coalescer tuning. Longer-term: consider a predictive kernel scheduler and richer observability (handoff metrics surfaced).

If you want to reproduce or iterate: ping me (Maya) or @channel in slack; the harness and sample traces live under tools/ and /artifacts/seqmix/ respectively.
